title: One For All: Achieving Adaptive Graph Neural Networks via Mixture of Message Passing

problem.claim: A single fixed message passing mechanism lacks the flexibility to handle graphs with differing node feature quality.

gap.claim: Existing GNN message passing mechanisms are fixed rather than adaptively selecting among different message passing mechanisms for individual edges.

contributions.claim: The paper proposes Mixture of Message Passing (MoMP), which incorporates a mixture-of-experts paradigm directly into GNN message passing.
MoMP uses a gating network for edge-level routing that adaptively selects a message passing expert for each edge.
MoMP introduces a partially shared expert architecture that reframes sparse-expert learning as a residual from a globally learned general mechanism.

stated_novelty.claim: The authors state that this is the first work to fuse the mixture-of-experts paradigm directly with the GNN message passing mechanism.

author_reported_evidence.claim: The authors report extensive experiments on several homophilic graph benchmarks.
The authors report that MoMP outperforms strong baselines on these benchmarks.
The authors report significant interpretability for the proposed method.

narrative_sequence.summary: Message passing is central to GNNs for capturing structural patterns.
Fixed message passing mechanisms show inconsistent performance across graphs with differing node feature quality.
MoMP applies mixture-of-experts message passing with edge-level gating and adaptive expert selection.
A partially shared expert architecture supports training sparse experts through residual learning from a globally learned mechanism.
Experiments on homophilic graph benchmarks are reported to show improved baseline performance and interpretability, while the authors characterize the fusion of MoE with GNN message passing as novel.

source_observation.claim: Fixed message passing mechanisms can perform inconsistently across graphs with differing node feature quality.

interpretation.claim: A model may benefit from adapting its local processing mechanism to graph-specific or edge-specific conditions.

application.claim: For heterogeneous graph workloads, consider routing individual messages among multiple specialized processing mechanisms.

exception.claim: The abstract reports experiments on homophilic graph benchmarks, so applicability to other graph regimes is unspecified.

unknowns: The abstract does not specify the benchmark datasets, baseline identities, or quantitative performance results.
The abstract does not describe the gating inputs, expert set, routing sparsity, or computational overhead.
The abstract does not provide details sufficient to assess the reported interpretability.
